summary: H.R. 10132, titled the ARTICLE ONE Act, changes how future national emergencies declared by the President take effect and operate. Under the bill, new national emergency declarations and their associated extraordinary powers automatically expire after 30 calendar days unless Congress passes a joint resolution of approval. It also sets up special fast-track congressional procedures for considering these resolutions, mandates detailed reports from the President to specific congressional entities every six months, and creates distinct rules for emergencies invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

affected_groups.effect: Must secure congressional approval via a joint resolution within 30 days to sustain new national emergency declarations or specific emergency powers, submit detailed periodic reports and cost estimates, and face restrictions on redeclaring identical emergencies if approval is denied.
Gains expedited procedures to review, debate, vote on, approve, or reject presidential national emergency declarations and renewals within strict calendar limits.
Must terminate contracts entered into under emergency authorities, and return unobligated reprogrammed or transferred funds to their original appropriations if a national emergency terminates.

key_provisions: Requires any new national emergency declaration and its specific emergency powers to expire after 30 calendar days unless a joint resolution of approval is enacted into law.
Prohibits the President from exercising emergency powers or authorities unless specific provisions of law are explicitly named in the emergency proclamation or an Executive order.

Limits the effective period of a renewed national emergency to one year unless the President submits an Executive order to renew it and Congress passes a joint resolution of approval before expiration.

Establishes expedited parliamentary procedures in both the Senate and the House of Representatives to consider joint resolutions of approval within strict timeframes, including committee discharge rules and limited debate.

Requires the President to submit written reports detailing circumstances, estimated durations, expected fund transfers, and estimated expenditures upon declaring or renewing an emergency, alongside periodic status updates every six months.
Excludes national emergencies invoking solely the International Emergency Economic Powers Act from these specific new title II procedures, moving prior provisions to a separate section.
missing_information: Exact criteria or definitions for what constitutes specific 'circumstances' preventing a presidential redeclaration after a failed approval.
Detailed internal mechanics of how specific committee jurisdictions will divide or handle resolutions outside of the named committees.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 10132, titled the ARTICLE ONE Act, changes how future national emergencies declared by the President take effect and operate. Under the bill, new national emergency declarations and their associated extraordinary powers automatically expire after 30 calendar days unless Congress passes a joint resolution of approval. It also sets up special fast-track congressional procedures for considering these resolutions, mandates detailed reports from the President to specific congressional entities every six months, and creates distinct rules for emergencies invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
summary_detail.significance: The bill shifts the balance of power between the executive and legislative branches regarding national emergencies. By replacing presidential emergency declarations that continue indefinitely unless actively blocked with a system requiring affirmative congressional approval within 30 days, the legislation creates a structured statutory review mechanism for future emergency powers. The significance score is 75 due to substantial institutional changes for executive authorities.
